newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria press hails Klima, warns hard tests ahead.
newsitem.headline: Austria press hails Klima, warns hard tests ahead.

text.p: Austrian newspapers on Monday welcomed the appointment of Viktor Klima as chancellor, but warned the golden boy of politics had a hard job ahead to solve the key issues of neutrality and the rise of the far right.
Klima, 49, apparently agreed with reluctance to take on the nation's top job after chancellor Franz Vranitzky unexpectedly announced his resignation on Saturday.

Most papers praised the speed with which Vranitzky, often criticised as wavering and indecisive, recognised his time was up and took his last bow from the political stage. The general consensus was that the move was a good thing.
Vranitzky had raised "strategic impotence" to a political principle during his time in office, a commentary in der Standard daily said.
A headline in Die Presse daily summed up Vranitzky's rule as: "One great success and many bad slip-ups."
Analysts are pinning their hopes on Klima's mix of toughness and charm to bring a much-needed breath of fresh air to what is seen as stale party leadership.
"Klima represents continuity but with different means. He is cleverer, more capable of getting the desired results and has a better instinct for power," the Kurier daily said.

Klima, 49, had proved his Machiavellian skill over the contentious sale of Creditanstalt bank last week, but in his new role as leader he still had to prove himself, a commentator in Der Standard said.
"The new strong man of Austria -- especially in these times of weakened coalition -- will have to give a sign very soon of his strength of character," it noted.
The paper's editorial said Vranitzky's government had been marked by the rapid rise of Joerg Haider, leader of the far-right Freedom Party over the past decade.
The Social Democrat vote slumped to an all-time low in European elections last October, dipping below 30 percent, while the far right support soared to nearly 28 percent.
Other papers focused on the future of foreign policy.
"Austria's international balance at the end of the Vranitzky era shows few concrete successes apart from European Union membership, but many failings," noted Die Presse.
"Security policy will soon demand decisions from Klima in an area he is unused to," it added.
While Vranitzky is credited with bringing the country into the EU in 1995, the issue of Austria's neutrality remains a bone of contention which Klima is likely to have to face.

The junior coalition partner, the conservative People's Party, has indicated it favours NATO membership, while the ruling Social Democrats have always maintained their determination to preserve the nation's neutral status.
The tabloid Taeglich Alles showed clear scepticism about the hasty leadership changeover.
"Mixed feelings: relief that the captain who kept the Austrian ship on its wavering course finally came ashore. There is uncertainty as to whether what comes after will be any better."
